Lecture 26

Equivariant line bundles and Borel–Weil

Lecture 12 induced from a character of a torus and obtained infinitely many irreducible representations. In this lecture a complex structure selects one of them. Induced representations act on equivariant functions, and the same functions can be read as sections of a vector bundle. We compute the holomorphic sections completely for the projective line. We then state the general Borel–Weil theorem, work the case SU⁡(3)\SU(3)SU(3) by hand, and prove the theorem from Peter–Weyl.

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

  • Compute all holomorphic sections of O(m)\mathcal O(m)O(m) on CP1\mathbb{CP}^1CP1.
  • Identify the resulting SU⁡(2)\SU(2)SU(2) representation and its central action.
  • State Borel–Weil with a specified bundle character and dual convention, and write explicit sections for SU⁡(3)\SU(3)SU(3).
  • Prove Borel–Weil from Peter–Weyl, and name the inputs that stay cited: G=KBG=KBG=KB, the complex structure of G/BG/BG/B, the character χλ\chi_\lambdaχλ​ and the highest-weight theorem.

26.1 From equivariant functions to sections

Let GGG be a Lie group, HHH a closed subgroup and σ:H→GL⁡(V)\sigma:H\to\GL(V)σ:H→GL(V) a continuous finite-dimensional complex representation. The quotient projection G→G/HG\to G/HG→G/H is a submersion by Lecture 3. So it has a smooth local section near every point of G/HG/HG/H, by the local-section theorem (Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, second edition, Theorem 4.26). We now attach a copy of VVV above each coset.

Definition 26.1. The associated vector bundle is E=G×HV=(G×V)/ ⁣∼,(gh,v)∼(g,σ(h)v).E=G\times_H V=(G\times V)/\!\sim,\qquad (gh,v)\sim(g,\sigma(h)v).E=G×H​V=(G×V)/∼,(gh,v)∼(g,σ(h)v). Its projection is [g,v]↦gH[g,v]\mapsto gH[g,v]↦gH. A section is a map s:G/H→Es:G/H\to Es:G/H→E whose value at xxx lies in the fibre above xxx. If dim⁡V=1\dim V=1dimV=1, it is a line bundle.

Each fibre is a vector space: choose ggg over the coset and use v↦[g,v]v\mapsto[g,v]v↦[g,v]. Changing ggg changes this identification by an invertible linear map.

Choose smooth local sections si:Ui→Gs_i:U_i\to Gsi​:Ui​→G whose domains cover G/HG/HG/H. The map Ui×V⟶E∣Ui,(x,v)⟼[si(x),v]U_i\times V\longrightarrow E|_{U_i},\qquad(x,v)\longmapsto[s_i(x),v]Ui​×V⟶E∣Ui​​,(x,v)⟼[si​(x),v] is a bijection, because every ggg over xxx has the form si(x)hs_i(x)hsi​(x)h with h∈Hh\in Hh∈H. It is linear on each fibre. On Ui∩UjU_i\cap U_jUi​∩Uj​, write sj(x)=si(x)hij(x)s_j(x)=s_i(x)h_{ij}(x)sj​(x)=si​(x)hij​(x). The same bundle vector then has coordinates vi=σ(hij)vj.v_i=\sigma(h_{ij})v_j.vi​=σ(hij​)vj​. The identity hijhjk=hikh_{ij}h_{jk}=h_{ik}hij​hjk​=hik​ ensures consistency on triple overlaps.

A smooth complex vector bundle of rank kkk over a manifold MMM is a smooth manifold EEE with a smooth surjection onto MMM and a complex vector-space structure on each fibre ExE_xEx​, the preimage of xxx. It is required to be locally a product. Each point of MMM has an open neighbourhood UUU and a diffeomorphism E∣U→U×CkE|_U\to U\times\C^kE∣U​→U×Ck mapping each fibre ExE_xEx​ complex-linearly onto {x}×Ck\{x\}\times\C^k{x}×Ck. These diffeomorphisms are the smooth local trivialisations.

These transition functions make E=G×HVE=G\times_HVE=G×H​V a smooth complex vector bundle, and this structure does not depend on the chosen family of local sections. The tool is the vector bundle chart lemma (Lee, Lemma 10.6). The section on sources at the end of this lecture checks its hypotheses.

It is well-defined because [gh,f(gh)]=[g,σ(h)f(gh)]=[g,f(g)].[gh,f(gh)]=[g,\sigma(h)f(gh)]=[g,f(g)].[gh,f(gh)]=[g,σ(h)f(gh)]=[g,f(g)]. Conversely, a section determines a unique f(g)f(g)f(g) in the coordinates supplied by ggg. Over UiU_iUi​, the section is x↦[si(x),f(si(x))]x\mapsto[s_i(x),f(s_i(x))]x↦[si​(x),f(si​(x))]. Moreover, sss is smooth exactly when fff is smooth, and sss is continuous exactly when fff is continuous. The section on sources gives the proof.

26.2 The projective line and its two charts

We first compute everything on one example, and we start with the holomorphic language it needs. A function on an open subset of Cd\C^dCd is holomorphic if it is real C∞C^\inftyC∞ and its differential is C\CC-linear at every point. Polynomials are holomorphic, and so are quotients of polynomials where the denominator is nonzero. Composition of holomorphic maps is holomorphic by the chain rule.

A complex manifold is a Hausdorff, second-countable topological space covered by charts. These charts are homeomorphisms of open sets onto open subsets of Cd\C^dCd. The transition maps between them have holomorphic components. A map between complex manifolds is holomorphic if it is continuous and its expressions in charts have holomorphic components.

Definition 26.2. The complex projective line CP1\mathbb{CP}^1CP1 is the set of one-dimensional complex subspaces of C2\C^2C2. A nonzero vector (v0,v1)(v_0,v_1)(v0​,v1​) determines the point [v0:v1][v_0:v_1][v0​:v1​], with [cv0:cv1]=[v0:v1][cv_0:cv_1]=[v_0:v_1][cv0​:cv1​]=[v0​:v1​] for c≠0c\ne0c=0.

There are two charts. On U0={v0≠0}U_0=\{v_0\ne0\}U0​={v0​=0} put z=v1/v0z=v_1/v_0z=v1​/v0​. On U1={v1≠0}U_1=\{v_1\ne0\}U1​={v1​=0} put w=v0/v1w=v_0/v_1w=v0​/v1​. On the overlap, the transition between the charts is w=1/zw=1/zw=1/z.

The charts give CP1\mathbb{CP}^1CP1 its topology. The points [1:0][1:0][1:0] and [0:1][0:1][0:1] have disjoint neighbourhoods {∣z∣<1}\{|z|<1\}{∣z∣<1} and {∣w∣<1}\{|w|<1\}{∣w∣<1}. Every other pair lies in a common chart, so the space is Hausdorff. The two charts give a countable base. Each chart is a copy of C\CC, and the transition w=1/zw=1/zw=1/z is holomorphic on the overlap. Hence the two charts make CP1\mathbb{CP}^1CP1 a complex manifold, in the sense above.

The group SU⁡(2)\SU(2)SU(2) acts on lines by matrix multiplication. In the zzz chart, the action of g=(a−bˉbaˉ)g=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&-\bar b\\b&\bar a\end{smallmatrix}\right)g=(ab​−bˉaˉ​) is z⟼b+aˉza−bˉzz\longmapsto\frac{b+\bar a z}{a-\bar b z}z⟼a−bˉzb+aˉz​ where the denominator is nonzero. The other chart expressions are similar. These rational expressions show that the action is smooth. It acts transitively. Indeed, a unit vector v=(a,b)v=(a,b)v=(a,b) is the first column of gv=(a−bˉbaˉ)∈SU⁡(2).g_v=\begin{pmatrix}a&-\bar b\\b&\bar a\end{pmatrix}\in\SU(2).gv​=(ab​−bˉaˉ​)∈SU(2). The stabiliser of the line C(1,0)\C(1,0)C(1,0) is T={tθ=diag⁡(eiθ,e−iθ)}.T=\{t_\theta=\diag(e^{i\theta},e^{-i\theta})\}.T={tθ​=diag(eiθ,e−iθ)}. By the homogeneous-space theorem of Lecture 3, CP1≅SU⁡(2)/T\mathbb{CP}^1\cong\SU(2)/TCP1≅SU(2)/T as smooth manifolds. It is compact, as the image of the compact group.

26.3 Computing the holomorphic sections

We import two results from complex analysis, the power-series theorem and Cauchy’s estimate. If fff is entire, then f(z)=∑k≥0akzk,∣ak∣≤R−kmax⁡∣z∣=R∣f(z)∣(R>0).f(z)=\sum_{k\ge0}a_kz^k,\qquad |a_k|\le R^{-k}\max_{|z|=R}|f(z)|\quad(R>0).f(z)=k≥0∑​ak​zk,∣ak​∣≤R−k∣z∣=Rmax​∣f(z)∣(R>0). Now we can say what holomorphy does. The Hilbert completion of the continuous induced representation of Lecture 12 is the space of all L2L^2L2 sections of O(m)\mathcal O(m)O(m). Let m≥0m\ge0m≥0. In physics language, O(m)\mathcal O(m)O(m) is the bundle of a charged particle on a sphere around a magnetic monopole, its two charts are two gauge patches, and the holomorphic sections are the lowest Landau level.

26.5 The general Borel–Weil theorem

We now replace SL⁡(2,C)\SL(2,\C)SL(2,C) and its upper triangular subgroup by a complex group GGG and a Borel subgroup BBB. The SU⁡(2)\SU(2)SU(2) case at the end of this section shows that the calculation above is the first instance.

A complex submanifold of a complex manifold MMM is a subset NNN with the following property. Each point of NNN lies in a chart of MMM in which NNN is given by the vanishing of some coordinates. The remaining coordinates give charts of NNN. Hence a holomorphic map into MMM with values in NNN is also holomorphic as a map into NNN. We call this the slice-chart property.

A complex Lie group is a group with a complex manifold structure for which multiplication and inversion are holomorphic. The groups KCK_\CKC​ of Lecture 14 are examples. A closed complex subgroup of a complex Lie group GGG is a closed subgroup that is also a complex submanifold.

Holomorphic bundles.

Suppose that GGG is a complex Lie group, HHH is a closed complex subgroup and G/HG/HG/H is a complex manifold. Suppose also that the projection π:G→G/H\pi:G\to G/Hπ:G→G/H is holomorphic, that σ\sigmaσ is holomorphic and that π\piπ has holomorphic local sections sis_isi​ whose domains UiU_iUi​ cover G/HG/HG/H. Then hij=si−1sjh_{ij}=s_i^{-1}s_jhij​=si−1​sj​ is holomorphic as a map into GGG, because the group operations of GGG are holomorphic. By the slice-chart property, hijh_{ij}hij​ is holomorphic as a map into HHH. Then σ(hij)\sigma(h_{ij})σ(hij​) is holomorphic, as a composition of holomorphic maps. So the local trivialisations given by the sections sis_isi​ make EEE a complex manifold. In this case EEE is a holomorphic vector bundle. These trivialisations are its holomorphic bundle charts, and the complex structure of EEE does not depend on the family (si)(s_i)(si​); the section on sources checks these points. A section is holomorphic when each coefficient f∘sif\circ s_if∘si​ is holomorphic.

A section is holomorphic exactly when its function f:G→Vf:G\to Vf:G→V is holomorphic. Indeed, if fff is holomorphic, then so is f∘sif\circ s_if∘si​. Conversely, the map q(g)=si(π(g))−1gq(g)=s_i(\pi(g))^{-1}gq(g)=si​(π(g))−1g on π−1(Ui)\pi^{-1}(U_i)π−1(Ui​) is holomorphic into HHH by the slice-chart property. The covariance (26.1) gives f(g)=σ(q(g))−1f(si(π(g))),f(g)=\sigma\bigl(q(g)\bigr)^{-1}f\bigl(s_i(\pi(g))\bigr),f(g)=σ(q(g))−1f(si​(π(g))), and both factors are holomorphic. Hence fff is holomorphic on each set π−1(Ui)\pi^{-1}(U_i)π−1(Ui​), and therefore on GGG.

The groups.

Let KKK be compact, connected, simply connected and semisimple. Its complexification G=KCG=K_\CG=KC​ was introduced in Lecture 14, and it is connected because KKK is. Fix a maximal torus TTT of KKK and positive roots. The positive Borel subalgebra b\mathfrak bb is the complex Cartan subalgebra plus the positive root spaces. Let BBB be the connected Lie subgroup of GGG with this Lie algebra.

We cite two facts about these groups. First, BBB is closed, and the inclusion of KKK in GGG induces a diffeomorphism from K/TK/TK/T onto the flag manifold G/BG/BG/B (Sepanski, Compact Lie Groups, Lemma 7.49 and Theorem 7.50). In particular, G=KB.G=KB.G=KB. Second, BBB is a closed complex subgroup, and G/BG/BG/B is a complex manifold with holomorphic projection π:G→G/B\pi:G\to G/Bπ:G→G/B and holomorphic local sections (Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras, Theorem 2.11 and its proof). So the paragraph on holomorphic bundles applies to GGG, BBB and G/BG/BG/B. The section on sources identifies Sepanski’s matrix model of GGG with the group of Lecture 14, and it proves that BBB is a complex subgroup.

The character.

Let λ\lambdaλ be an integral weight. Since KKK is simply connected, X∗(T)=PX^*(T)=PX∗(T)=P (Lecture 7). Let N+N_+N+​ be the connected subgroup of GGG whose Lie algebra is the sum of the positive root spaces. Each b∈Bb\in Bb∈B is uniquely a product texp⁡(iH)nt\exp(iH)ntexp(iH)n with t∈Tt\in Tt∈T, H∈tH\in\algtH∈t and n∈N+n\in N_+n∈N+​, and these factors depend smoothly on bbb (Sepanski, Lemma 7.49(d)). Our character of weight λ\lambdaλ on TTT is exp⁡H↦eiλ(H)\exp H\mapsto e^{i\lambda(H)}expH↦eiλ(H). Define χλ:B→C×\chi_\lambda:B\to\C^\timesχλ​:B→C× by χλ(exp⁡(H′)exp⁡(iH)n)=eiλ(H′)−λ(H)(H,H′∈t, n∈N+).\chi_\lambda\bigl(\exp(H')\exp(iH)n\bigr)=e^{i\lambda(H')-\lambda(H)}\qquad(H,H'\in\algt,\ n\in N_+).χλ​(exp(H′)exp(iH)n)=eiλ(H′)−λ(H)(H,H′∈t, n∈N+​). We import from Sepanski, Definition 7.52, the fact that this formula defines a homomorphism. The formula is well defined on T=exp⁡tT=\exp\algtT=expt because λ∈P=X∗(T)\lambda\in P=X^*(T)λ∈P=X∗(T). By the smooth dependence of the factors on bbb, the homomorphism χλ\chi_\lambdaχλ​ is smooth. It is trivial on N+N_+N+​. Left translations of BBB are holomorphic, and χλ\chi_\lambdaχλ​ is multiplicative. So its differential is C\CC-linear at every point, and χλ\chi_\lambdaχλ​ is holomorphic.

The bundle.

Define Lλ=G×BC−λ,(gb,u)∼(g,χλ(b)−1u).L_\lambda=G\times_B\C_{-\lambda},\qquad (gb,u)\sim(g,\chi_\lambda(b)^{-1}u).Lλ​=G×B​C−λ​,(gb,u)∼(g,χλ​(b)−1u). Sections correspond to functions with f(gb)=χλ(b)f(g).\begin{equation} \label{lec26:bwcov} f(gb)=\chi_\lambda(b)f(g). \end{equation}f(gb)=χλ​(b)f(g).(26.4) A section is holomorphic exactly when its function f:G→Cf:G\to\Cf:G→C is holomorphic. Theorem 26.4 (Borel–Weil). With the preceding positive Borel and bundle convention, if λ\lambdaλ is dominant integral, then H0(G/B,Lλ)≅Vλ∗H^0(G/B,L_\lambda)\cong V_\lambda^*H0(G/B,Lλ​)≅Vλ∗​ as a KKK-representation. This is finite-dimensional and irreducible. If an integral λ\lambdaλ is not dominant, then H0(G/B,Lλ)=0H^0(G/B,L_\lambda)=0H0(G/B,Lλ​)=0.

The proof below uses the cited facts about BBB, χλ\chi_\lambdaχλ​ and G/BG/BG/B above, in particular G=KBG=KBG=KB. It also uses the holomorphic extension of Lecture 14 and the highest-weight theorem of the prerequisite course. The rest comes from the Peter–Weyl theorem.

The dual Vλ∗V_\lambda^*Vλ∗​ has highest weight −w0λ-w_0\lambda−w0​λ. Here w0w_0w0​ is the longest element of the Weyl group, the element that sends the positive roots to the negative roots. For SU⁡(n)\SU(n)SU(n), the element −w0-w_0−w0​ reverses the Dynkin labels. For SU⁡(2)\SU(2)SU(2) we have −w0λ=λ-w_0\lambda=\lambda−w0​λ=λ, so the dual is invisible there.

The case SU⁡(3)\SU(3)SU(3) by hand

Here G=SL⁡(3,C)G=\SL(3,\C)G=SL(3,C), and BBB is the subgroup of upper triangular matrices. A flag is a line ℓ\ellℓ inside a plane PPP in C3\C^3C3. Figure 26.3 shows one. The case SU⁡(2)\SU(2)SU(2)

For K=SU⁡(2)K=\SU(2)K=SU(2) the group GGG is SL⁡(2,C)\SL(2,\C)SL(2,C) (Lecture 14), and BBB is the subgroup of upper triangular matrices in GGG. The character is χm(b)=cm,b=(cβ0c−1)∈B.\chi_m(b)=c^m,\qquad b=\begin{pmatrix}c&\beta\\0&c^{-1}\end{pmatrix}\in B.χm​(b)=cm,b=(c0​βc−1​)∈B. It is trivial on the unipotent matrices, where c=1c=1c=1. On the diagonal matrices it is diag⁡(c,c−1)↦cm\diag(c,c^{-1})\mapsto c^mdiag(c,c−1)↦cm, the character of weight mmm. The fibre at C(1,0)\C(1,0)C(1,0) transforms by c−mc^{-m}c−m. The map gB↦[g(1,0)T]gB\mapsto[g(1,0)^T]gB↦[g(1,0)T] identifies G/BG/BG/B with CP1\mathbb{CP}^1CP1. Self-checks

1. What is wrong with choosing an arbitrary entire f0f_0f0​ as a section of O(1)\mathcal O(1)O(1)?

Answer. The coefficient f1(w)=wf0(1/w)f_1(w)=wf_0(1/w)f1​(w)=wf0​(1/w) must also extend holomorphically to w=0w=0w=0. This forces f0f_0f0​ to have degree at most one.

2. Which representation occurs in H0(CP1,O(3))H^0(\mathbb{CP}^1,\mathcal O(3))H0(CP1,O(3))?

Answer. It is Sym3(C2)∗≅V3\mathrm{Sym}^3(\C^2)^*\cong V_3Sym3(C2)∗≅V3​, of dimension four and spin 3/23/23/2. The central element −I-I−I acts by the scalar (−1)3=−1(-1)^3=-1(−1)3=−1, so this representation does not descend to SO⁡(3)\SO(3)SO(3).

3. Does LλL_\lambdaLλ​ always produce highest weight λ\lambdaλ in our general convention?

Answer. No. Its section space is Vλ∗V_\lambda^*Vλ∗​, of highest weight −w0λ-w_0\lambda−w0​λ, where w0w_0w0​ is the longest element of the Weyl group. For SU⁡(2)\SU(2)SU(2) these weights coincide. For SU⁡(n)\SU(n)SU(n), the element −w0-w_0−w0​ reverses the Dynkin labels, so for SU⁡(3)\SU(3)SU(3) the bundle L(1,0)L_{(1,0)}L(1,0)​ gives highest weight (0,1)(0,1)(0,1).

Summary

Equivariant functions correspond to sections of associated bundles. On CP1\mathbb{CP}^1CP1 and for m≥0m\ge0m≥0, the transition rule for O(m)\mathcal O(m)O(m) identifies holomorphic sections with homogeneous polynomials of degree mmm. Compact induction contains Vm,Vm+2,…V_m,V_{m+2},\dotsVm​,Vm+2​,…, and holomorphy keeps only VmV_mVm​. For compact, connected, simply connected, semisimple KKK, the Borel–Weil theorem gives H0(G/B,Lλ)≅Vλ∗H^0(G/B,L_\lambda)\cong V_\lambda^*H0(G/B,Lλ​)≅Vλ∗​ for dominant integral λ\lambdaλ, and zero otherwise. We proved it from Peter–Weyl. Covariance and holomorphy make the vectors in each coefficient block highest weight vectors of weight λ\lambdaλ, so only one block survives. The facts G=KBG=KBG=KB, the complex structure of G/BG/BG/B, the character χλ\chi_\lambdaχλ​ and the highest-weight theorem stay cited. For SU⁡(3)\SU(3)SU(3), first-column and wedge coordinates give explicit sections.

Smooth structure of associated bundles.

We show that E=G×HVE=G\times_HVE=G×H​V is a smooth complex vector bundle. The local sections sis_isi​ are smooth, so the maps hij=si−1sjh_{ij}=s_i^{-1}s_jhij​=si−1​sj​ are smooth into GGG. They take values in the embedded subgroup HHH, so they are smooth into HHH by the codomain-restriction result for embedded submanifolds [C: Lee, Corollary 5.30]. The representation σ\sigmaσ is smooth by the automatic-smoothness theorem of Lecture 3. Hence the transition functions σ(hij)\sigma(h_{ij})σ(hij​) are smooth. Let k=dim⁡Vk=\dim Vk=dimV, choose a basis of VVV, and regard Ck\C^kCk as R2k\R^{2k}R2k. Each fibre of EEE is then a real vector space of dimension 2k2k2k, and the real matrices of σ(hij)\sigma(h_{ij})σ(hij​) are smooth maps into GL⁡(2k,R)\GL(2k,\R)GL(2k,R). The vector bundle chart lemma [C: Lee, Lemma 10.6] applies to these real data. It gives EEE a unique topology and smooth structure for which the inverses of the maps above are smooth local trivialisations. These maps are complex-linear on fibres, so EEE is a smooth complex vector bundle.

This structure does not depend on the chosen family of local sections. For a second family (sj′)(s'_j)(sj′​), the maps si−1sj′s_i^{-1}s'_jsi−1​sj′​ are smooth into HHH by the same codomain-restriction argument. So the mixed transition functions σ(si−1sj′)\sigma(s_i^{-1}s'_j)σ(si−1​sj′​) are smooth, and the chart lemma applies to the union of the two families. By its uniqueness clause, the union gives the same structure as each family alone.

Holomorphic inverse functions.

Let Φ\PhiΦ be a map between open subsets of Cd\C^dCd with holomorphic components and invertible differential at a point. The real inverse function theorem gives a smooth local inverse. Its differential is the inverse of a C\CC-linear map, hence C\CC-linear. So the local inverse is holomorphic. This is the holomorphic inverse function theorem.

The Borel subgroup and the quotient.

By Sepanski, Definition 7.48, BBB is the connected Lie subgroup of GGG with Lie algebra b\mathfrak bb. By Sepanski, Lemma 7.49, BBB is closed. By Sepanski, Theorem 7.50, the inclusion induces a diffeomorphism from K/TK/TK/T onto G/BG/BG/B.

Since BBB is closed, it is an embedded Lie subgroup of GGG by the closed-subgroup theorem of Lecture 3. The inclusion of BBB with Sepanski’s Lie subgroup structure is smooth into this embedded submanifold by Lee, Corollary 5.30. It is a bijective Lie group homomorphism, so it is a Lie group isomorphism by Lee, Corollary 7.6. Hence the embedded group BBB has Lie algebra b\mathfrak bb, and exp⁡\expexp maps some neighbourhood OOO of 000 in b\mathfrak bb diffeomorphically onto an open subset of BBB.

Choose a complex complement m\mathfrak mm of b\mathfrak bb in g\mathfrak gg. For b∈Bb\in Bb∈B, define Φ:b×m→G\Phi:\mathfrak b\times\mathfrak m\to GΦ:b×m→G by Φ(X,Y)=bexp⁡Xexp⁡Y.\Phi(X,Y)=b\exp X\exp Y.Φ(X,Y)=bexpXexpY. The matrix exponential is holomorphic and maps g\mathfrak gg into GGG, so Φ\PhiΦ is holomorphic into GGG by the slice-chart property. Its differential at (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) is the complex-linear isomorphism (X,Y)↦b(X+Y)(X,Y)\mapsto b(X+Y)(X,Y)↦b(X+Y). By the holomorphic inverse function theorem, after shrinking OOO, there is a neighbourhood O′O'O′ of 000 in m\mathfrak mm such that Φ\PhiΦ maps O×O′O\times O'O×O′ biholomorphically onto an open set W′⊂GW'\subset GW′⊂G. The set Φ(O×{0})=bexp⁡O\Phi(O\times\{0\})=b\exp OΦ(O×{0})=bexpO is open in BBB. Because BBB has the subspace topology, it equals B∩W′′B\cap W''B∩W′′ for some open set W′′W''W′′. On W=W′∩W′′W=W'\cap W''W=W′∩W′′, the set BBB is exactly the slice Y=0Y=0Y=0. Hence BBB is a closed complex subgroup.

The complex quotient theorem [C: Kirillov Jr., Theorem 2.11 and its proof] makes G/BG/BG/B a complex manifold, with holomorphic projection π:G→G/B\pi:G\to G/Bπ:G→G/B and holomorphic local sections. Thus the first section applies to GGG, BBB and G/BG/BG/B.

Hence χm(h01)=z−m\chi_m(h_{01})=z^{-m}χm​(h01​)=z−m.

Let f:G→Cf:G\to\Cf:G→C satisfy f(gb)=χm(b)f(g)f(gb)=\chi_m(b)f(g)f(gb)=χm​(b)f(g), and put f0=f∘s0f_0=f\circ s_0f0​=f∘s0​ and f1=f∘s1f_1=f\circ s_1f1​=f∘s1​. Since s1(1/z)=s0(z)h01s_1(1/z)=s_0(z)h_{01}s1​(1/z)=s0​(z)h01​, covariance gives f1(1/z)=f(s0(z)h01)=z−mf0(z)(z≠0).f_1(1/z)=f\bigl(s_0(z)h_{01}\bigr)=z^{-m}f_0(z)\qquad(z\ne0).f1​(1/z)=f(s0​(z)h01​)=z−mf0​(z)(z=0). With w=1/zw=1/zw=1/z, this is the transition rule f1(w)=wmf0(1/w)f_1(w)=w^mf_0(1/w)f1​(w)=wmf0​(1/w) of O(m)\mathcal O(m)O(m).

Next we compare the two complex structures on G/BG/BG/B. Write π:G→G/B\pi:G\to G/Bπ:G→G/B for the projection, and identify G/BG/BG/B with CP1\mathbb{CP}^1CP1 by gB↦[g(1,0)T]gB\mapsto[g(1,0)^T]gB↦[g(1,0)T]. The vector g(1,0)Tg(1,0)^Tg(1,0)T is the first column (g11,g21)T(g_{11},g_{21})^T(g11​,g21​)T of ggg. Hence π−1(U0)={g11≠0}\pi^{-1}(U_0)=\{g_{11}\ne0\}π−1(U0​)={g11​=0} and π−1(U1)={g21≠0}\pi^{-1}(U_1)=\{g_{21}\ne0\}π−1(U1​)={g21​=0} are open in GGG. In the charts, z∘π(g)=g21g11on π−1(U0),w∘π(g)=g11g21on π−1(U1).z\circ\pi(g)=\frac{g_{21}}{g_{11}}\quad\text{on }\pi^{-1}(U_0),\qquad w\circ\pi(g)=\frac{g_{11}}{g_{21}}\quad\text{on }\pi^{-1}(U_1).z∘π(g)=g11​g21​​on π−1(U0​),w∘π(g)=g21​g11​​on π−1(U1​). These are quotients of holomorphic functions with nonvanishing denominators. Hence π\piπ is holomorphic for the chart structure. The sections s0s_0s0​ and s1s_1s1​ are holomorphic for the chart structure, because their entries are polynomials. By the comparison of the two group structures above, the cited structure on G/BG/BG/B also makes π\piπ holomorphic for the submanifold structure on GGG, and it has holomorphic local sections.

Let sss be a holomorphic local section for one of the two structures. Then π∘s\pi\circ sπ∘s is the identity map on the domain of sss. This composition is holomorphic into the other structure, because π\piπ is holomorphic for that structure. Applying this in both directions shows that the identity map of G/BG/BG/B is holomorphic with holomorphic inverse. Hence the two complex structures coincide.

Let s′s's′ be another holomorphic local section over an open subset of U0U_0U0​. Then q=s0−1s′q=s_0^{-1}s'q=s0−1​s′ takes values in BBB, and it is holomorphic into BBB by the slice-chart property. Covariance gives f∘s′=χm(q)f0f\circ s'=\chi_m(q)f_0f∘s′=χm​(q)f0​. The factor χm(q)\chi_m(q)χm​(q) is holomorphic and nowhere zero, so it does not change holomorphy. The same holds over U1U_1U1​. Hence a section of LmL_mLm​ is holomorphic exactly when f0f_0f0​ and f1f_1f1​ are entire.

This is the agreement of the two notions of holomorphic section that the projective-line calculation uses.

Reading

  • M. R. Sepanski, Compact Lie Groups (2007), Section 7.4: the Borel–Weil theorem and the groups GGG and BBB.

  • J. M. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, second edition (2013), Chapters 4, 5 and 10: local sections, embedded submanifolds and the vector bundle chart lemma.

  • T. Bröcker and T. tom Dieck, Representations of Compact Lie Groups (1985), Sections III.4 and III.8: faithful representations and complexification.
